NEW YORK (CNN) -- A massive anti-Mafia sweep that stretched from New York to Sicily has not only cut off the head of the Gambino crime family but lopped off "the shoulders and chest" too, prosecutors said Thursday. John "Jackie the Nose" D'Amico, shown in 1992, is one of 62 people indicted. Sixty-two members of the Gambino, Genovese and Bonanno families face 80 charges, ranging from money laundering to illegal gambling and murder. "These charges strike at the very core of the Gambino family," said Benton Campbell, United States attorney for the Eastern District of New York. The Gambino family profited from extortion within the New York construction industry and its labor unions, according to the charges.  Watch the perp walk » . Several companies allegedly paid a "mob tax" in return for "protection" and "permission to operate," said Gordon Heddell, inspector general of the U.S. Department of Labor. Other charges involve an alleged illegal gambling ring, said Richard Brown, Queens County district attorney. Nicholas Corozzo -- a reputed captain in the Gambino family -- was involved in a sports gambling enterprise that relied in part on toll-free telephones, Brown alleged. Meanwhile, four members of the Gambino family are charged with eight crimes involving murder, according to the indictment. Those charges include the felony murder of Jose Delgado Rivera, who was shot and killed in an armored truck during a robbery in 1990. "Today we are able to bring closure to crimes from the past that have never been forgotten," Campbell said. He said the crimes span back over three decades.  Watch feds say they've 'cut off the head' of crime family » . Key to the Gambino arrests Thursday was a member of the Attorney General's Organized Crime Task Force who infiltrated the Gambino family and recorded hundred of hours of conversations, said John Milgrim, a spokesman for the attorney general. Forty-five of those charged are already in custody, police said. Arrests were made in New York City; Long Island, New York; and New Jersey. "It is as unrelenting as weeds that continue to sprout in the cracks of society," New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo said of organized crime. "We will not rest until organized crime is a distant memory." In addition to the arrests in the New York area, police in Italy detained 77 people in connection with organized crime. Those arrests netted important members of a powerful clan in Sicily linked to Mafia boss Salvatore Lo Piccolo, who was believed to be the successor of the boss of bosses, Bernardo Provenzano.  Watch the prosecutor explain why authorities acted now » . Police say that in his attempt to rise to power, Le Piccolo tried to mend fences with New York-based Mafia families after those ties were broken during the bloody Mafia wars of the 1980s. Those families included the Gambinos of New York and the Inzerillos of Italy. Provenzano was arrested two years ago in Corleone. "It is evident that the intent of the Mafia in Palermo was to re-establish a dialogue through the Inzerillo family in the U.S," Francesco Messineo of the Italian Police said. "A dialogue that was never interrupted because the relationship between the American and the Italian Mafia is historic, based on long tradition. But there was certainly an attempt to re-establish that connection." Investigators believe mob clans wanted to collaborate on illegal commercial ventures such as money laundering and drug trafficking. Italian officials said the arrests were aimed at preventing these illegal activities, but they warned that other Mafia clans in Sicily oppose the return of the Inzerillo family to the island, and therefore were concerned about a new Mafia war. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Deborah Feyerick and Alessio Vinci contributed to this report.

**U.S. and Italian authorities arrest top suspects in major transatlantic crackdown on Gambino crime family**

By **CNN Staff**

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Federal agents in New York and law enforcement officers in Palermo, Sicily, executed a coordinated, pre-dawn sweep Wednesday, dealing a heavy blow to the infamous Gambino crime family and its deep-rooted network in the Sicilian Mafia.

The joint international operation resulted in the arrest of 16 suspects—10 in the United States and six in Italy—who face a slew of federal charges including racketeering conspiracy, extortion, arson, witness tampering, and assault. 

The 16-count indictment, unsealed in federal court in Brooklyn, paints a vivid picture of a modern-day mob syndicate that relies on old-school violence, threats, and intimidation to control legitimate industries, particularly garbage hauling and demolition in the New York metropolitan area.

"For decades, the Gambino crime family has attempted to project an image of untouchability, but today’s arrests prove once again that international borders will not protect organized crime from the long arm of the law," said Breon Peace, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, during a press conference Wednesday morning. 

"These defendants engaged in a ruthless pattern of violent extortion, arson, and witness intimidation—all to line their pockets and maintain their chokehold on local businesses," Peace added.

### Violent extortion and 'old-world' intimidation

According to court documents, the Gambinos systematically targeted business owners in the carting and construction sectors. Prosecutors allege that members of the crime family demanded recurring "protection" payments—often referred to as a "tribute"—from victims.

In one instance detailed in the indictment, mob associates allegedly torched a business in New Jersey after the owner refused to pay extortion demands. In another case, defendants allegedly threatened to dismember a victim and beat an employee with a hammer to enforce compliance.

Among those arrested in New York is Joseph Lanni, also known as "Joe Brooklyn," an alleged captain, or *caporegime*, in the Gambino organization who prosecutors say orchestrated much of the local extortion scheme.

At the same time federal agents were making arrests in New York and New Jersey, the Italian State Police (*Polizia di Stato*) launched synchronized raids across Palermo, targeting high-ranking members of the Sicilian Cosa Nostra who provided structural support, money laundering channels, and muscle for the American operations.

"The bond between the New York mafia and Sicilian organized crime remains active and dangerous," said Maurizio de Lucia, Chief Anti-Mafia Prosecutor for Palermo. "This operation demonstrates that our alliance with American law enforcement is stronger than the criminal pacts binding these mafiosi across the Atlantic."

### A historic connection revisited

The Gambino crime family—historically one of the "Five Families" that dominated organized crime in New York City—has long maintained blood and business ties to the Sicilian Mafia. While law enforcement crippled much of the Mafia's high-level leadership during the 1980s and 1990s, officials say Wednesday's arrests prove the syndicate has quietly attempted to rebuild its influence.

FBI Assistant Director-in-Charge James Smith emphasized that while the techniques may have adapted to the 21st century, the core operations of the mob remain unchanged.

"The Mob may have tried to lower its profile, but its methods remain rooted in fear, violence, and greed," Smith said. "Working side-by-side with our Italian counterparts, we have disrupted a transatlantic criminal enterprise that thought it was operating in the shadows."

If convicted, several of the defendants face maximum sentences ranging from 20 years to life in prison. 

The defendants arrested in the U.S. are scheduled to make their initial court appearances in Brooklyn federal court Wednesday afternoon, while extradition proceedings for those detained in Italy are expected to begin in the coming days.

**SPECIAL REPORT**

**OPERATION OLD BRIDGE: FBI AND ITALIAN POLICE CRIPPLE GAMBINO CRIME FAMILY IN TRANSATLANTIC MOB BUST**

**NEW YORK — February 7, 2008** — In one of the most devastating blows to organized crime in a generation, hundreds of federal agents and police officers launched pre-dawn raids across New York City, Long Island, and Italy today, effectively decapitating the leadership of the Gambino crime family. 

Code-named **"Operation Old Bridge,"** the massive coordinated sweep resulted in federal indictments against 62 defendants in the United States and more than 20 suspects in Palermo, Sicily. The raids targeted the top tier of the Gambino hierarchy, laying bare a sprawling web of extortion, racketeering, cold-case murders, and a dangerous new alliance between American mobsters and the Sicilian Mafia.

Officials say the operation has neutralized the ruling panel that has run the Gambino family since the downfall of infamous boss John Gotti.

---

### **Decapitating the High Command**

Among those named in the 170-page federal indictment unsealed in Brooklyn were the three highest-ranking members of the Gambino administration:

*   **Domenico "Italian Dom" Cefalù**, 61, the family’s Underboss.
*   **Joseph "Miserable" Corozzo**, 66, the family’s Consigliere (counselor).
*   **Nicholas "Little Nick" Corozzo**, 67, the reputed Acting Boss. *(Corozzo evaded capture during the initial morning raids after being tipped off, though federal agents apprehended him weeks later).*

Also swept up in the raid were high-ranking captains (caporegimes), including **Frank Cali**, a rapidly rising star with deep ties to the Sicilian Mafia, and **Charles Carneglia**, a notorious Gambino enforcer linked to multiple decades-old murders.

"Today, we knocked out the leadership structure of the Gambino crime family," said Benton Campbell, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, during a press conference in Brooklyn. "This operation is the culmination of years of hard work by federal and international law enforcement agencies."

---

### **The Wiretap and the Informant**

The downfall of the Gambino high command was made possible by an insider who broke the Mafia's oath of silence (*omertà*). 

The key to the investigation was **Joseph Vollaro**, a truck company owner and Gambino associate facing severe drug charges. To avoid a lengthy prison sentence, Vollaro agreed to become a confidential informant for the FBI. For nearly three years, Vollaro wore a concealed recording device during secret meetings with top mobsters. 

Vollaro captured hundreds of hours of incriminating conversations. The recordings provided extraordinary insight into the family’s day-to-day operations, including:
*   **Extortion in the Construction Industry:** Systematic shakedowns of construction firms operating in New York, including lucrative extortion rackets tied to the attempted development of a NASCAR racetrack in Staten Island.
*   **Union Corruption:** Deep infiltration and control over local truck drivers and construction unions.
*   **Illegal Gambling and Loansharking:** Massive illegal bookmaking operations and exorbitant interest rates charged to desperate debtors.

---

### **Cold Cases and Bloodshed Solved**

While much of the indictment focused on financial racketeering, the charges against veteran mob hitman **Charles Carneglia** exposed the bloody history of the Gambino family dating back to the 1970s. 

Carneglia was charged with participating in five brutal murders, including:
1.  **Albert Gelb (1976):** A Court Officer who had arrested Carneglia in a diner. Gelb was shot to death days before he was scheduled to testify against him.
2.  **Michael "Mickey Boy" Paradiso (1983):** Murdered over a dispute regarding a drug operation.
3.  **John Rohr (1990) and Louis DiBono (1990):** DiBono was a Gambino soldier killed on the orders of John Gotti; his body was found in a body bag inside a car parked beneath the World Trade Center.
4.  **Jose Delgado Rivera (1990):** An armored car guard killed during a robbery at Brooklyn's MetroTech Center.

According to court documents, Carneglia routinely boasted to associates about how he disposed of bodies, allegedly using acid to dissolve the remains of his victims in a cement yard.

---

### **The "Old Bridge": A Re-Emergence of the Sicilian Mafia**

What set Operation Old Bridge apart from previous American mob busts was its transatlantic scope. The operation was named after the physical and historical "bridge" connecting the Brooklyn-based Gambinos to their roots in Palermo, Sicily.

Simultaneous raids conducted by the Italian State Police in Sicily targeted the **Inzerillo clan**. During the 1980s, the Inzerillos were driven out of Palermo during a bloody Mafia war waged by the ruthless Corleonesi faction, led by Salvatore "Totò" Riina. Surviving members of the Inzerillo family fled to New York, where they were protected by the Gambinos and earned the nickname "The Zips."

Federal prosecutors revealed that in recent years, caporegime Frank Cali had been negotiating to allow the exiled Inzerillos to return to Sicily and reclaim their territory. Law enforcement intercepted intelligence showing that the two factions were attempting to reactivate a high-level heroin trafficking pipeline across the Atlantic—reminiscent of the infamous "Pizza Connection" of the 1980s.

"This investigation proves that the link between La Cosa Nostra in the United States and the Mafia in Italy remains strong and dangerous," said Francesco Gratteri, director of the Italian anti-mafia police unit.

---

### **The Aftermath and the Decline of La Cosa Nostra**

Operation Old Bridge was hailed by federal authorities as the final nail in the coffin for the era of mob dominance established by John Gotti in the late 1980s. 

Mark Mershon, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI’s New York Field Office, struck a triumphant tone: *"If there was any doubt that La Cosa Nostra is a dying institution, today’s arrests should lay that doubt to rest once and for all."*

While legal experts caution that the Mafia has proven resilient in the past, the simultaneous loss of the Gambinos' top bosses, key earners, and hitmen—combined with the destruction of their lucrative Italian narcotics connection—leaves the Gambino family in its weakest state since its founding in the early 20th century.

**Feds deal massive blow to NY Mafia, charging more than 60 members of Gambino, Genovese, and Bonanno families**

**By John Miller and Kara Scannell, CNN**  
Updated 11:42 AM EDT, Thu October 24, 2024

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Federal prosecutors on Thursday unsealed a sweeping, 82-count indictment charging more than 60 members and associates of the Gambino, Genovese, and Bonanno crime families, dealing what law enforcement officials called one of the most significant blows to La Cosa Nostra in New York in over a decade.

Early morning raids executed across New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut resulted in the arrests of dozens of high-ranking mobsters, including capos, soldiers, and associates. The defendants face a laundry list of charges, including racketeering conspiracy, extortion, labor union corruption, loan sharking, and wire fraud. 

**Watch the perp walk »**

"Today’s arrests prove that La Cosa Nostra is far from a relic of the past," Damian Williams, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, said at a Thursday morning news conference. "The mob may have modernized its methods, but their core business remains the same: extortion, violence, and greed. If you choose the path of organized crime, federal law enforcement will track you down."

According to court records, the joint investigation—code-named "Operation Broken Throne"—was conducted over four years by the FBI, the NYPD, and the Department of Labor. Investigators utilized wiretaps, undercover agents, and thousands of hours of secret surveillance to dismantle the multi-family operation.

**RELATED STORY: How the FBI infiltrated a secret Gambino social club in Brooklyn »**

Prosecutors allege that while the three families operated distinct crews, senior members collaborated on several major schemes. Among the primary allegations is a massive labor racketeering plot in which members of the Genovese family allegedly infiltrated a local construction union, using threats of physical violence to secure lucrative kickbacks and siphon millions from employee health funds.

Meanwhile, members of the Gambino family were charged with operating an offshore illegal sports gambling ring that processed tens of millions of dollars in illicit wagers using illegal websites based in Costa Rica.

**Watch: FBI official details how three rival mob families collaborated »**

Among those named in the indictment are alleged Gambino family capo Frank "Frankie Boy" Ruggiero and senior Bonanno soldier Anthony "The Fish" Corrado. Prosecutors allege Ruggiero personally directed a protection racket that forced small business owners in Brooklyn and Manhattan’s Little Italy to pay monthly "tributes" under threat of arson and assault.

In one wiretapped conversation detailed in the indictment, a defendant is allegedly heard threatening a local restaurant owner: "You pay us every month, or your building burns down before the weekend. It’s that simple."

**Hear the secret wiretap audio released by federal prosecutors »**

"Organized crime acts as a tax on honest businesses and a blight on our communities," said Christie Curtis, Acting Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI's New York Field Office. "The myth of the untouchable mobster is just that—a myth."

Attorneys for several of the defendants denied the charges outside the courthouse on Thursday, maintaining their clients' innocence. 

The defendants are scheduled to make their initial court appearances in federal court in Manhattan on Thursday afternoon. If convicted on the top racketeering conspiracy charges, several high-ranking members face up to 20 years in federal prison.

counterfactuals.prompt: What were the key findings and international connections revealed during the federal crackdown on John "Jackie the Nose" D'Amico and the Gambino crime family?
counterfactuals.output:
The federal crackdown on John "Jackie the Nose" D'Amico and the Gambino crime family culminated in **Operation Old Bridge** in February 2008. This massive, joint U.S.-Italian law enforcement operation resulted in the indictment of 62 individuals in the United States and dozens more in Italy. 

At the time, D'Amico was serving as the street boss (or acting boss) of the Gambino family, sharing power in a panel that included Nicholas "Little Nick" Corozzo and Joseph "Miserable" Corozzo.

The crackdown yielded major findings regarding the modern inner workings of the American Mafia and exposed extensive, re-established international connections between New York's La Cosa Nostra and the Sicilian Mafia.

Here are the key findings and international connections revealed by the investigation:

---

### 1. Key Findings of the Crackdown

* **Decapitation of the Gambino Leadership Structure:**
  The operation dismantled the top echelon of the Gambino family. D'Amico, along with consigliere Joseph Corozzo and several high-ranking captains (caporegimes), was arrested. This forced the family into a period of severe instability and leadership turnover.

* **Infiltration of Major Infrastructure and Construction Projects:**
  The indictments revealed that the Gambino family retained a stranglehold on New York’s construction and waste-hauling industries. A prominent finding was the family’s extortion scheme surrounding a proposed **NASCAR / Formula One racetrack on Staten Island** (which was ultimately canceled). The Gambinos had systematically extorted trucking and dirt-hauling contractors working on the site.

* **Resolution of Cold-Case Murders:**
  Wiretaps and cooperating witnesses allowed federal prosecutors to solve several high-profile mob murders dating back decades. These included:
  * The 1977 murder of Albert Gelb, a New York State court officer who had arrested a Gambino mobster.
  * The 1998 murder of Frank Hydell, who was killed outside a Staten Island strip club because he was suspected of cooperating with the FBI.

* **Pervasive Union Corruption and Extortion:**
  The investigation documented widespread extortion of construction companies, labor union locals (particularly related to the Teamsters and cement leagues), and illegal gambling rings that netted the family millions of dollars annually.

* **Crucial Role of Informants:**
  The crackdown relied heavily on **Joseph Vollaro**, a Gambino associate turned confidential informant. Facing long prison time on drug charges, Vollaro wore a wire for years, secretly recording hundreds of hours of conversations with D'Amico, the Corozzo brothers, and other high-ranking mobsters detailing extortion, loansharking, and internal mob politics.

---

### 2. International Connections Revealed (The Sicilian Alliance)

The most groundbreaking aspect of Operation Old Bridge was its exposure of **resurrected ties between the Gambino crime family and the Sicilian Mafia (Cosa Nostra)**, which had been largely severed during the bloody Sicilian Mafia wars of the 1980s.

* **The Return of *Gli Scappati* (The Runaways):**
  During the Second Mafia War in Sicily (1981–1984), the brutal Corleonesi faction (led by Totò Riina) slaughtered the rival **Inzerillo clan**. Surviving members of the Inzerillo family fled to New York, where they were sheltered by their relatives, the Gambinos. They became known in Italy as *gli scappati* (the runaways). 
  * *The Finding:* By the mid-2000s, with Riina in prison, the Gambinos were actively helping the Inzerillos return to Palermo, Sicily, to reclaim their lost territories, assets, and power within the Sicilian Mafia.

* **Transatlantic Envoys and Secret Summits:**
  Wiretaps revealed that high-level envoys were regularly traveling between New York and Palermo to coordinate strategy. 
  * Gambino soldier Thomas Cacciopoli and others were dispatched to Sicily to meet with top Sicilian bosses like Salvatore Lo Piccolo and Gianni Nicchi.
  * Sicilian mobsters traveled to New York under the guise of legitimate business to meet with D’Amico and his inner circle to iron out alliances.

* **New International Drug Trafficking and Money Laundering Routes:**
  The investigation proved that the Gambinos and the Sicilian Mafia were planning to re-establish large-scale international narcotics trafficking routes (similar to the historic "Pizza Connection" of the 1970s and 80s). They were also coordinating cross-border money laundering schemes using legitimate European businesses and real estate.

* **Precedent-Setting FBI-Italian Police Cooperation:**
  Operation Old Bridge marked a historical milestone in international law enforcement. The U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI worked in direct, real-time synchronization with the Italian State Police (*Polizia di Stato*) and the Anti-Mafia District Directorate (*DDA*) of Palermo. Agents were cross-stationed in Rome, Palermo, and New York, executing simultaneous raids at 6:00 AM on both sides of the Atlantic.

---

### Summary of Impact

The crackdown on John D'Amico's faction demonstrated that despite decades of federal prosecutions under the RICO Act, the Gambino family remained a formidable criminal enterprise. However, it also proved that the mob's attempt to modernize by forging a new transatlantic alliance with Sicily was thoroughly compromised by modern surveillance and law enforcement cooperation. D'Amico eventually pleaded guilty to racketeering extortion charges in 2008 and was sentenced to prison, further accelerating the decline of the traditional Italian-American Mafia structures in New York.

counterfactuals.output:
**TRANSATLANTIC MAFIA CRACKDOWN: FBI AND ITALIAN POLICE BUST TRANSNATIONAL PLOT TO REBUILD HISTORIC NY-SICILY CRIME BRIDGE**

**NEW YORK & PALERMO, Italy** — In a coordinated early-morning sweep spanning two continents, federal agents and Italian police arrested more than two dozen alleged mobsters on Tuesday, dismantling a sophisticated attempt to re-establish the historic "bridge" between the New York Mafia and Sicilian Cosa Nostra.

Dubbed "Operation Transatlantic Alliance," the multi-year joint investigation resulted in 19 arrests in the New York metropolitan area and 11 in Palermo, Sicily. Defendants face sweeping federal and international indictments, including racketeering conspiracy, international narcotics trafficking, extortion, and money laundering.

According to unsealed court documents filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York, high-ranking members of New York’s Gambino and Bonanno crime families were actively working with Palermo’s powerful Passo di Rigano and Inzerillo clans. Law enforcement officials say the alliance sought to modernize traditional criminal pipelines to traffic narcotics and launder tens of millions of dollars through luxury real estate, olive oil imports, and cryptocurrency networks.

"Today’s operation sends an unmistakable message: the Atlantic Ocean is not a safe zone for organized crime," said U.S. Attorney Breon Peace during a joint press conference in Brooklyn. "These defendants attempted to resurrect a dark legacy of transatlantic criminal collaboration. Thanks to unprecedented cooperation between U.S. and Italian law enforcement, that bridge has been dismantled before it could fully take hold."

**A Historic Connection Restored—and Broken**

The historic ties between the Sicilian Mafia and American Cosa Nostra date back decades, notably culminating in the "Pizza Connection" drug rings of the 1970s and 80s. Ties were severely fractured following internal Mafia wars in Sicily and a series of devastating federal prosecutions in the United States.

However, intelligence gathered over the past three years revealed a concerted effort by a new generation of mobsters to reconnect the two factions. Investigators utilized court-authorized wiretaps, financial audits, and physical surveillance to track high-level meetings disguised as routine business trips.

Surveillance photos released by the FBI show American capos meeting with Sicilian bosses at luxury hotels in Miami and quiet trattorias on the outskirts of Palermo. 

"The Cosa Nostra in Palermo was seeking to regain its global financial foothold by leveraging deep-rooted familial and structural ties in New York," said Chief Prosecutor Maurizio de Lucia of the Palermo Anti-Mafia Directorate. "They believed that by using encrypted communication applications and modern business fronts, they could operate under the radar of international law enforcement. They were mistaken."

**Drugs, Money Laundering, and Extortion**

According to the indictment, the conspiracy involved a plan to establish a steady pipeline of high-grade cocaine shipped from South America through Sicilian ports, destined for distribution in the New York tri-state area. In return, the American factions provided access to sophisticated money-laundering schemes, utilizing shell companies based in Delaware and Manhattan to clean illicit proceeds.

The indictments also allege that the syndicate engaged in old-world extortion tactics, demanding *pizzo*—protection money—from Italian business owners operating in Brooklyn, Queens, and Long Island who had family ties in Sicily. 

Among those arrested in New York was Vito "The Baker" Ruggiero, an alleged acting captain in the Gambino family, who prosecutors describe as a key liaison between the American and Sicilian factions. In Palermo, authorities detained several members of the resurrected Inzerillo clan, whose predecessors fled to New York in the 1980s during the rise of the brutal Corleonesi faction.

**Next Steps**

The American defendants are scheduled to make their initial court appearances in Brooklyn federal court later this afternoon, where prosecutors are expected to argue for detention without bail, citing the defendants as severe flight risks with deep international connections. Extradition proceedings for several suspects arrested in Italy are expected to begin in the coming weeks.

If convicted on the top racketeering and drug conspiracy charges, several high-ranking defendants face maximum sentences of life in prison.

Law enforcement officials from both countries emphasized that while today’s raids represent a major blow to traditional organized crime, financial audits and secondary investigations into the network's asset holdings remain ongoing.
